sources.title: JCGM 100:2008, Evaluation of measurement data — Guide to the expression of uncertainty in measurement (BIPM, 2008 corrected version), 134 PDF pages
sources.locator: Clause 3.1–3.3, clause 4.1.1–4.1.4 (measurement model and input quantities), clause 4.2 (Type A evaluation), clause 4.3 (Type B evaluation), clause 5.1.1–5.1.5 (uncorrelated inputs, equations (10)–(12)), clause 5.2.1–5.2.2 (correlated inputs, equation (13)), clause 6.2 (expanded uncertainty), Annex B.2.13–B.2.15, Annex C.2.9–C.2.13 and C.3.4–C.3.6

contents.name: 4.1.1–4.1.2 The functional relationship Y = f(X1, ..., XN) (equation (1)) and the requirement that f contain every significant correction quantity
contents.support: The measurement-model definition records the open input domain, the Borel model function, the input random element and the output quantity, and states that corrections and additional input quantities are model data.

contents.name: 4.1.3 Categorization of input quantities: those determined in the measurement and those brought in from calibrated standards and reference data
contents.support: The calibration definition records reference inputs supplied by a standard, reference observations and a rule selecting apparatus settings, with reference uncertainty carried in the datum.

contents.name: 4.2 Type A evaluation of standard uncertainty from repeated observations, the arithmetic mean and the experimental standard deviation of the mean
contents.support: The repeated-observation sampling model records the family of real observations with the adopted IID and second-moment hypotheses and defines the sample mean; the quantitative mean/variance statements are the published corollary cited in the remark.

contents.name: 4.3 Type B evaluation from calibration certificates, specifications and reference data
contents.support: The calibration datum absorbs Type B information as the stated reference uncertainty of the reference inputs; no separate quantitative Type B model is built.

contents.name: 5.1.1–5.1.3 Combined standard uncertainty, equation (10), sensitivity coefficients and the law of propagation of uncertainty
contents.support: The lemma proves the finite-sample covariance identity A Σ A^T for the linearization, which is the exact algebraic content of the first-order propagation law for a declared random input vector.

contents.name: Note to 5.1.2: higher-order terms when the nonlinearity of f is significant (quantified in example H.1)
contents.support: The corollary supplies the explicit second- and fourth-moment domination of the second-order Taylor remainder under a uniform Hessian bound, which is the direction the note requires.

contents.name: 5.2.1–5.2.2 Correlated input quantities and equation (13)
contents.support: The covariance-matrix definition and its symmetry and positive-semidefiniteness proof supply the off-diagonal covariance data that equation (13) requires.

contents.name: 6.2 Expanded uncertainty and the coverage factor k
contents.reason: An expanded-uncertainty interval with a coverage probability requires a stated distribution or quantile supplier (for example a normal law and its convolution); the page provides only the distribution-free covariance and moment bounds, so no expanded-uncertainty interval is built.

contents.name: B.2.13 Corrected result (result after correction for systematic error)
contents.reason: The corrected-result bookkeeping presumes a systematic-error correction procedure that is part of a consuming physical measurement model; the mathematics page records only that corrections are additional model inputs.

contents.name: B.2.14 Accuracy of measurement (closeness of agreement with a true value)
contents.reason: Accuracy is explicitly a qualitative concept in the source and is not used by any item: no numerical accuracy claim is made about a calibrated map.

contents.name: B.2.15 Repeatability of results of measurements and the repeatability conditions
contents.support: The repeated-observation sampling model records repeated observation of one quantity as an adopted model hypothesis rather than deriving it from the qualitative repeatability condition.

contents.name: C.2.9 Expectation of a random variable
C.2.11–C.2.12 Variance and standard deviation of a random variable
C.2.13 Central moments and the second central moment
C.3.4 Covariance of two random variables
C.3.5 Covariance matrix: diagonal entries are variances and off-diagonal entries are covariances
contents.support: The definition identifies Σii = Var(Xi) and proves symmetry and positive semidefiniteness of the vector covariance matrix.

contents.name: C.3.6 Correlation coefficient
contents.reason: The normalized correlation coefficient is not used by this page; the covariance matrix already records all second-order information the propagation results require.

sources.title: B. N. Taylor and C. E. Kuyatt, Guidelines for Evaluating and Expressing the Uncertainty of NIST Measurement Results, NIST Technical Note 1297 (1994), 27 PDF pages
sources.locator: Sections 1–6 (error and uncertainty, Type A and Type B evaluation, combined standard uncertainty, expanded uncertainty, reporting) and Appendix A, equations (A-1)–(A-5)

contents.name: Section 2 Measurement result as an estimate of the value of the measurand, with subsection 2.3 distinguishing error from uncertainty
contents.support: The remark records that model data such as σ² is not a measured error bar and that error and measured outcome are distinct notions in the consuming physical item.

contents.name: Section 3 Type A evaluation of standard uncertainty based on statistical methods for treating data (including the standard deviation of the mean, equation (A-5))
contents.support: The sampling model supplies the hypotheses under which a standard deviation of the mean is a model quantity; its quantitative form is the published IID corollary.

contents.name: Section 4 Type B evaluation from previous data, experience, specifications, calibration reports and reference data
contents.support: Type B information enters as the stated reference uncertainty in the calibration datum; no independent Type B probability model is developed.

contents.name: Section 5 Combined standard uncertainty and the law of propagation of uncertainty (root-sum-of-squares)
contents.support: The lemma proves the propagated covariance A Σ A^T for the declared random input vector, including the correlated case.

contents.name: Section 6 Expanded uncertainty and the coverage factor k
contents.reason: As with the corresponding GUM clause, a coverage factor converts a standard uncertainty into an interval only under a stated distributional or quantile hypothesis, which this page does not supply.

contents.name: Appendix A, equation (A-3) u_c^2(y) as the double sum of sensitivity coefficients, variances and covariances (first-order Taylor approximation)
contents.support: The lemma proves exactly the quadratic-form identity in the finite-sample setting, with the covariance matrix defined and its entries proved finite.

contents.name: Appendix A, equation (A-4) sample mean of n independent observations under the same conditions
contents.support: The sampling model defines the sample mean of the observation family.

sources.title: JCGM 200:2012, International Vocabulary of Metrology — Basic and General Concepts and Associated Terms (VIM), 3rd edition, 108 PDF pages
sources.locator: Clause 2, definition 2.39 (calibration) with Note 1, definition 2.40 (calibration hierarchy), and clause 4.1 (indication)

contents.name: 2.39 Calibration: establishing a relation between reference quantity values with uncertainties and indications, then using the information to obtain a measurement result from an indication
contents.support: The definition records a calibration family, reference inputs with stated uncertainty, reference observations and a rule selecting apparatus settings, exactly the structure the VIM calibration operation describes.

contents.name: 2.39 Note 1: a calibration may be expressed by a statement, function, diagram, curve or table and may consist of an additive or multiplicative correction with associated uncertainty
contents.support: The calibration rule is stated as an arbitrary map on admissible reference data, so a correction table or function is one admissible instance.

contents.name: 2.40 Calibration hierarchy
contents.reason: Traceability chains and institutional calibration hierarchies are metrological organization, not mathematics used by this page's propagation and sampling results.

contents.name: 4.1 Indication (quantity value provided by a measuring instrument or measuring system)
contents.reason: The indication is physical apparatus output; the mathematical observation variable and its error slot are already defined, and no separate indication model is consumed.

sources.title: L. Wasserman, All of Statistics: A Concise Course in Statistical Inference (Springer, 2004), 458 PDF pages; full-text copy at the cited URL
sources.locator: Section 5.5 (delta method), Section 6.2–6.3 (parametric models, confidence sets, hypothesis testing, examples 6.13–6.17), Section 9.3 with Definition 9.7 (likelihood), Section 10.1 (power function and size, Definition 10.1) and Section 10.2 (p-values and the interpretive warnings)

contents.name: Section 5.5 The delta method: asymptotic normality of a smooth function of an estimator via a first-order expansion
contents.support: The corollary is the finite-sample counterpart of the delta method's first-order expansion; the asymptotic normality the delta method assumes is not available on this page and is not used.

contents.name: Section 6.3.2 Confidence sets, display (6.9): P_theta(theta in Cn) >= 1 - alpha for all theta, and the coverage terminology
contents.support: The definition generalizes intervals to arbitrary confidence sets with the measurability condition and states the coverage level as an infimum.

contents.name: Example 6.14 (after Berger and Wolpert, 1984): a 75 percent confidence interval that is a single point on some data, with the warning that a confidence interval is not a probability statement about theta
contents.support: The counterexample reconstructs the witness as a finite model, verifies coverage 3/4 by enumeration and exhibits a datum with conditional probability 1.

contents.name: Theorem 6.16 Normal-based confidence interval and Example 6.17 Bernoulli interval
contents.reason: The normal-based interval requires a central limit theorem and normal quantiles, which this page does not supply; the distribution-free sampling bound is used instead.

contents.name: Section 6.3.3 Hypothesis testing: null and alternative hypotheses and the rejection-region convention
contents.support: The test definition records the model family, the null set and the rejection region and derives the size from them.

contents.name: Section 9.3 and Definition 9.7 The likelihood function as the joint density of the data viewed as a function of the parameter
contents.support: The definition states the likelihood for a family of densities relative to a fixed dominating measure, without any estimate or asymptotic claim.

contents.name: Sections 9.4–9.14 Properties, consistency, asymptotic normality and optimality of maximum likelihood estimators
contents.reason: The asymptotic theory of maximum likelihood requires regularity and convergence suppliers that this page does not build, and no consumer here estimates a parameter by maximum likelihood.

contents.name: Definition 10.1 Power function beta(theta) = P_theta(X in R), size alpha = sup over Theta_0 of beta, and the level convention
contents.support: The definition reproduces the power function, the size as a supremum over the null set and the level convention with their nonemptiness and boundedness conditions.

contents.name: Section 10.2 p-values, Theorem 10.12 and the warnings that a large p-value is not evidence for the null and that the p-value is not P(H0 | Data)
contents.support: The remark records the interpretive warning for the page's test and confidence definitions; no p-value item is built because the page does not develop test statistics or their null distributions.

contents.name: Theorem 10.14 Uniformity of the p-value under a continuous null distribution
contents.reason: The uniformity statement requires continuous null distributions and is not used: no p-value distribution is computed on this page.

sources.title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, chapter 7 (Product and Process Comparisons), sections 7.1.3–7.1.5
sources.locator: Section 7.1.3 (what are statistical tests?), section 7.1.4 (what are confidence intervals?) and section 7.1.5 (relationship between a test and a confidence interval), read from the chapter's section pages

contents.name: 7.1.3 Statistical tests: null hypothesis, test statistic, critical values and the rejection decision
contents.support: The definition formalizes the rejection decision as membership in a measurable rejection region of a specified family.

contents.name: 7.1.4 Confidence intervals: a stated confidence level means that in repeated sampling the constructed intervals bracket the parameter in approximately that fraction of cases
contents.support: The definition states the coverage level as an infimum of the model probabilities P_theta(theta in C) over the parameter set.

contents.name: 7.1.5 The correspondence between a level-alpha test and a level 1-alpha confidence interval
contents.support: The remark records that both constructions are properties of the same specified family and adds the data-conditional warning; no separate interval-construction theorem is built.

sources.title: S. Greenland, S. J. Senn, K. J. Rothman, J. B. Carlin, C. Poole, S. N. Goodman and D. G. Altman, 'Statistical tests, P values, confidence intervals, and power: a guide to misinterpretations', European Journal of Epidemiology 31 (2016), 337–350
sources.locator: Abstract, introduction, the section 'Statistical tests, P values, and confidence intervals: a caustic primer' (statistical models, hypotheses and tests; uncertainty, probability and statistical significance), and the explanatory list of 25 misinterpretations (groups on P values, interval comparisons and predictions, confidence intervals, and power)

contents.name: Primer: every inference method depends on a statistical model whose assumptions include the sampling or randomization protocol, and many assumptions go unremarked
contents.support: The remark states that the page's definitions are conditional on their specified family and transport no protocol or preparation assumptions.

contents.name: Primer: frequentist probability refers to hypothetical frequencies of data patterns under an assumed model, not to probabilities of hypotheses; likelihood refers to the probability of the observed data given the parameter
contents.support: The remark states that a likelihood value is not a probability of the parameter value and that no distribution on the parameter set is part of the definitions.

contents.name: Misinterpretations of single P values (the P value is not the probability that the test hypothesis is true; non-significance is not evidence for the null)
contents.support: The remark records the corresponding warning for the page's test-size definition and asserts no posterior or truth probability.

contents.name: Misinterpretations of confidence intervals (the realized interval is not a probability statement about the fixed parameter; the level is not a posterior probability of the parameter)
contents.support: The counterexample exhibits a level-3/4 set with conditional probability 1 for a declared prior and datum, and the remark records the general warning.

contents.name: Misinterpretations of power (observed power is not the power of the test; non-significance plus high post hoc power is not evidence for the null)
contents.reason: The page does not develop power calculations, effect sizes or sample-size planning, so the power-related misinterpretations have no corresponding construction here.

contents.name: Guidelines for improving statistical interpretation and reporting
contents.reason: Reporting guidelines concern the presentation of empirical studies; this mathematics page states model-conditional results and makes no reporting or editorial recommendation.

sources.title: Rick Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th edition (2019 working draft), 490 pages
sources.locator: Section 1.6.3 (variance var(X) = E(X - EX)^2), Theorem 1.6.4 (Chebyshev's inequality), Section 2.1 (independence of finitely many random variables), Section 2.2.1 (i.i.d. sequences, the variance of a sum of independent variables and the L2 weak law, Theorem 2.2.3), Section 3.10, 'Limit Theorems in R^d', Theorem 3.10.7 (finite covariances Gamma_ij = E((X_{n,i} - mu_i)(X_{n,j} - mu_j)) of a random vector)

contents.name: 1.6.3 Variance of a real random variable, var(X) = E(X - EX)^2, and its scaling law
contents.support: The sampling model adopts the same finite-second-moment convention; the quantitative mean/variance statements are the published root corollary cited in the remark.

contents.name: 1.6.4 Chebyshev's inequality
contents.support: The example's displayed sample-mean bound is this inequality in the i.i.d. normalization; the proof route of the example is the local second-moment identity.

contents.name: 2.1 Independence of finitely many random variables (product form of joint probabilities)
contents.support: The IID hypothesis of the sampling model is the same independence convention applied to the observation family.

contents.name: 2.2.1 i.i.d. sequences, variance of a sum of independent variables, and the L2 weak law (Theorem 2.2.3)
3.10 'Limit Theorems in R^d', Theorem 3.10.7: finite covariances Gamma_ij of a random vector
contents.support: The definition records the same covariance-matrix convention for a random vector; well-definedness under square-integrability is proved locally.

sources.title: K. Bryan, Taylor's Theorem in One and Several Variables (Rose-Hulman MA 433 lecture notes), 4 pages
sources.locator: First-order case in n dimensions (equation (4)), second-order case in n dimensions (equation (8)) with its proof (equations (9)-(10)), and the Hessian matrix form

contents.name: Second order case of Taylor's theorem in n dimensions (equation (8)): f(x) = f(a) + grad f(a) . (x-a) + 1/2 (x-a)^T H(b) (x-a) for some b on the segment from a to x
contents.support: The lemma bounds the Hessian remainder term by (B/2)|y-mu|^2 under a uniform operator-norm bound on the Hessian, which is exactly the displayed Lagrange form of the second-order remainder.

contents.name: Matrix form of the second-order term with the Hessian matrix H
contents.support: The example verifies equality and strictness of the (B/2)|y-mu|^2 bound for h(y)=y^2 and g(y)=y^3.

contents.name: First order case in n dimensions (equation (4)) and the one-dimensional preliminaries
contents.reason: The first-order expansion is supplied by the published total-derivative and Jacobian items and by lem-cm-linearized-propagation-of-covariance; no new first-order statement is taken from this source.

sources.title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, section 7.1.3, 'What are statistical tests?'
sources.locator: Section 7.1.3 (What are statistical tests?): null hypothesis, test statistic, critical values, rejection; one-sided and two-sided alternatives

contents.name: What is meant by a statistical test? Null hypothesis, test statistic, critical values, rejection
contents.support: The definition records the rejection region of a specified model family and its size; the source's procedural description motivates the same vocabulary without asserting that any apparatus meets the model.

contents.name: Concept of null hypothesis; one-sided tests of hypothesis
contents.support: One- and two-sided null and alternative hypotheses correspond to different null sets Theta_0 and rejection regions; the definition covers both through the family and the supremum over Theta_0.
